title: Learning to Choose: Where AI Literacy Begins
author: Jennifer W. Shewmaker
summary: Jennifer Shewmaker opens a new series that shifts attention from what teachers set as AI expectations to the decisions students must learn to make for themselves. Beginning with a student deciding late at night whether to ask an AI tool to write an assignment, she argues that a syllabus policy and a prompting lesson are not enough. Students need an examined ethical framework that connects their beliefs about learning, honesty and responsibility to ordinary choices. She draws on C. S. Lewis's image of looking through a beam of light rather than at it, and on her earlier work on students' fear of learning and on classroom hospitality. Examples from a middle school writing project at Summit Christian School and from a Lipscomb University tutoring bot show AI used as a tool rather than a crutch. She closes with a practical routine: before students open an AI tool, have them name what they are trying to learn, then afterward explain whether their choices served that learning.
points: The author claims that policy and prompt skills are insufficient, because in the moment a student needs to understand what she is asking the tool to do and why.
The Lewis image of looking through a beam of light, not at it, frames the point that written values only matter when they steer decisions made while tired and behind.
Contrasting two students shows that the same tool can deepen learning (testing an explanation against the text) or replace it (summarising instead of reading).
She argues that deliberately choosing not to use AI is a legitimate, explainable decision, and students should be able to justify abstaining as well as using.
The recommended practice is simple: name the learning goal before opening the tool, then review afterward whether the help served it.
quotes: I’ve become convinced that students need to begin developing their own ethical framework early in that work. They need practice connecting what they believe about learning, honesty, and responsibility to the choices that they make daily on ordinary assignments.

Students can write a statement about what they value, just like looking directly at that beam of light. But the harder work is learning to let those values guide a decision when they are tired, uncertain, and a due date is looming.

In the first case, he has done the reading and uses AI to work through a question, while in the second the student comes to class without having read it at all. These are clearly different uses of AI that lead to differing levels of learning.
Instead of having AI rewrite his essay, he learned to use it to work through the problems and clarify the questions.

A useful framework should help students ask those questions before they act and to recognize situations in which they need guidance. They may be uncertain about permission, about the reliability of an answer, or about whether information belongs in a particular tool.
We also want students to understand that choosing not to use AI can be a deliberate, informed decision. They may need to develop a skill through independent practice.

Eventually, they will face choices for which no teacher or professor has written instructions, and most certainly as AI progresses, their circumstances and tools will change. They will need convictions they have examined and judgment they have practiced.
